name: Prussian Union and the Old Lutherans
summary: King Frederick William III's union of the Lutheran and Reformed churches of Prussia, and his government's persecution of the 'Old Lutherans' who refused it, many of whom emigrated to America and Australia.

start.label: Frederick William III calls for a united Lutheran and Reformed church for the Reformation's 300th anniversary

end.label: Frederick William IV's 'General Concession' legally recognizes the Old Lutherans

key_dates.label: King's new common liturgy (Agende) enforced at the 300th anniversary of the Augsburg Confession
Troops force open the church at Hönigern, Silesia, for the union liturgy (December)
Old Lutheran emigrations to Australia (1838) and the United States (1839) begin

background.text: The Hohenzollern kings were Reformed while most of their subjects were Lutheran; Frederick William III wanted one Protestant church and personally wrote much of its new liturgy.

happened.text: The union began as voluntary in 1817, but the king's common liturgy (1822) was pressed on congregations, and from 1830 refusing it became a punishable offense.

Led by Johann Gottfried Scheibel of Breslau, 'Old Lutherans' who insisted on the Lutheran confessions and liturgy refused; their pastors were suspended, fined, and jailed, and services were held in secret.
Thousands emigrated: Pastor August Kavel led groups to South Australia from 1838, and Pastor J. A. A. Grabau led others to Buffalo, New York, in 1839.

participants.name: Frederick William III
participants.role: King of Prussia who imposed the union

participants.name: Johann Gottfried Scheibel
participants.role: Breslau theologian who led the resistance

participants.name: J. A. A. Grabau
participants.role: Pastor imprisoned for resistance; founded the Buffalo Synod

participants.name: August Kavel
participants.role: Pastor who led emigrants to South Australia

outcomes.text: The emigrants helped found confessional Lutheran churches in America and Australia, and the controversy strengthened confessional Lutheranism, including the Missouri Synod.
The Evangelical Church of the Prussian Union lasted, in changing forms, until the 2000s; the Old Lutherans in Germany are part of today's Independent Evangelical-Lutheran Church (SELK).

condemnations.authority: Evangelical Church in Prussia (under the king)
condemnations.reason: Old Lutheran pastors, including Scheibel and Grabau, suspended or deposed for refusing the union liturgy

persecution.title: Suppression of the Old Lutherans
persecution.summary: Pastors who refused the union were removed, fined, and imprisoned; Grabau was jailed in 1837–38. In December 1834 soldiers forced open the church at Hönigern in Silesia and installed a union pastor; worshippers who resisted were beaten and soldiers quartered on them. Lay people who held secret services were fined and had property seized.

responsible.name: Prussian consistories
responsible.role: Church authorities who enforced the union

persecution.outcome: Thousands emigrated; persecution ended after the king's death in 1840.

sources.citation: Christopher Clark, "Confessional Policy and the Limits of State Action: Frederick William III and the Prussian Church Union 1817–40," Historical Journal 39 (1996).
